title: Justice Department’s interference before midterms was unsuccessful, unprofessional and unprecedented
paragraphs: From Washington, D.C. to Anchorage, Alaska, federal courts have been busy with cases related to the Trump administration’s attempts to assert control over state elections. In almost every case, rulings have gone against the administration. But despite the fears of many Democrats, there was no mayhem launched by the Trump administration on Election Day.

One federal judge chastised administration officials for being “engaged in a campaign to intimidate, threaten and coerce state and local officials and employees who are engaged in administering the ongoing midterm 2026 election.” Another wrote with umbrage that “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger.” And the nation’s highest court, the Supreme Court, in what The New York Times called “an extraordinary rebuke,” refused to intervene in the administration’s appeal of a lower court ruling that barred federal intervention in California ballot counting.

The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor, Naomi Schalit, spoke on Election Day with Dickinson College President John Jones, a former federal judge, about the Trump administration’s actions – and how judges see them.
What are you seeing with all these cases?

The common stripe in every one of the cases that have been decided close to the election is that courts are reluctant to get involved after voting has started. And I think the courts’ perspectives are clearly affected by the high number of early votes cast either in person before Election Day or using mail-in voting. Without question, we’ve already been in the midst of this election – from a voting standpoint – for some time, and courts simply don’t want to get in the way of that and disrupt the process.
The court opinions haven’t been only about how they don’t want to get involved. They’re also saying to the Justice Department, “You shouldn’t be taking a role here as well.”

That’s right. And of course it harkens back to what I’ve said before, which is that Article 1, Section 4 of the Constitution gives the states the power to regulate elections. Congress has some license to legislate in matters relating to national elections, but notably absent from Section 4 is any role for the executive branch to play.

All of the cases have that perspective. But as you go case by case, even assuming that the administration could, for example, sell its allegation that there are 20,000 suspect ballots in California and that the administration has an interest in those ballots, it’s simply too close to the election. There is something called the Purcell Principle, based on a Supreme Court precedent, that federal courts as a rule should not wade into election controversies at a point in time that’s too close to when they’re being conducted.
What does the string of administration losses in these cases tell you about the leadership at the Department of Justice?

I believe that the Department of Justice has become completely unmoored from its mission. Recall that in 2016, very close to the presidential election, then-FBI Director James Comey revealed the investigation into candidate Hillary Clinton’s emails.

It was seen as a tremendous breach of protocol by the Department of Justice. And look at where we are today, where it has now become the norm for the Department of Justice to take action so close to the election.

Just today, for example, we know that target letters were sent out by the Department of Justice to numerous individuals allegedly involved in the Alaska controversy that placed a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. There were a thousand or so election watchers dispatched to polling places by the Department of Justice – these are unprecedented numbers.

Then there were the lawsuits that were filed by the Department of Justice close to the election. This was forbidden territory for the DOJ before this election cycle, and it’s now become business as usual.
It was forbidden territory because the idea was that – unlike most of the other executive agencies – the DOJ had a kind of holy, nonpolitical status?

The central idea, I think, is that the Department of Justice would not want to put its thumb on the scale and affect an election, particularly if there’s an investigation that is announced and isn’t closed.

To reveal an investigation – or investigations, as they’ve done in several cases now – means that some will take that as meaning there has been criminal misconduct when that obviously may not be the case at all. This is a further weaponization of the Department of Justice, in my view, that I find unconscionable.

And given how clumsy its efforts have been, this is clearly the leadership of the Department of Justice acceding to the wishes of the president of the United States even when there is no sound legal basis to proceed. A lot of this has been very unprofessionally done and strains both the reputation and credibility of the Department of Justice and the lawyers that it’s sending in front of federal judges.

Given the number of judges’ rulings declaring that the administration’s positions are contrary to the Constitution, is the leadership of the DOJ susceptible – given the Democrats have gotten the majority in the House – to impeachment for not fulfilling their oath, which requires them to support and defend the Constitution of the United States?

I don’t know that this is going to ripen to the extent that impeachment is suggested as a remedy, although arguably it could be. But I can easily see that this is going to be the subject of intensive investigations as to who ordered what and when they ordered it. And people are going to be subpoenaed and asked questions under oath that may be difficult to answer.
What is it like for these judges to be dealing with this barrage of cases that are so big and so consequential?

Typically, judges can operate under pressure; I did that many times. You’re equipped to do that as a federal judge. The real drag on the system right now is the absence of the presumption of regularity judges are being faced with. Lawyers are failing to tell the truth under direct questioning by judges. This is really an astonishing development.

Government lawyers are not litigating to the professional standards that once were the hallmark of the department. A tremendous drag on the system is caused when judges hear lawyers telling them things that simply defy belief. And they are being intentionally disingenuous as well.

And then you have to do what some judges are now doing, which is connecting the dots and issuing orders where they are expressly saying what the judge’s areas of concerns are. It’s like spoon-feeding lawyers, which judges really don’t like to do. They expect a higher degree of professionalism.
When you litigate in the federal courts, you should bring your A game – all the time. You’re playing in the big leagues.

title: Democrats in House poised to investigate the Trump Administration, taking up a long-standing power GOP-led Congress ignored for the past two years
paragraphs: Oversight is coming for the Trump administration.

That’s been the message of congressional Democrats throughout the closing days of the 2026 midterm campaign. Now that the party’s candidates have reportedly won control of the House of Representatives, that campaign promise is likely to be carried out. Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin told The New York Times in late October that among the potential oversight targets were pardons granted by President Donald Trump, possible corruption in government contracting and the Trump family’s cryptocurrency deals.
Routine congressional oversight hearings usually don’t make headlines.
That changed during the second Trump administration.
When Attorney General Pam Bondi appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Oct. 7, 2025, what took place was a contentious, highly partisan, made-for-TV-and-social-media confrontation.
Bondi refused to answer many questions from Democrats, instead launching personal attacks against these members of the U.S. Senate.
The episode captures a basic tension in congressional oversight: Congress can demand answers, but getting them often depends on the cooperation of the branch it is investigating.
That tension is about to sharpen when Democrats control the oversight process. Their hearings will likely be anything but routine.
From our perspective as political scientists who study the U.S. Congress, congressional oversight has played an important role in American democracy. Here’s a brief history.

In simple terms, oversight is the ability of Congress to ensure that the laws it passes are faithfully executed. This generally means asking questions, demanding information, convening hearings and holding the executive branch accountable for its actions.

Oversight isn’t specifically mentioned in the Constitution. Article 1, Section 8, which lists the powers of Congress, includes the power “to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper,” without identifying an oversight role. Once laws are enacted, Article 2, Section 3, states that the president “shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.”

However, the framers viewed congressional oversight as a key component of legislative authority. They wanted presidents to take Congress seriously and structured the Constitution to ensure that the executive would be accountable to the legislature.

As James Madison urged in Federalist 51, the separate branches of government should have the power to keep each other from becoming too powerful. “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” Madison wrote.

The framers drew from the examples of the British Parliament and Colonial legislatures. In 1621, Sir Francis Bacon was charged with corruption and impeached as Lord High Chancellor after an investigation by a committee of the British Parliament. And in 1768, the Massachusetts Assembly conducted an investigation of Gov. Francis Bernard that led to a formal request to the King of England for his removal.

At the Federal Convention in 1787 that produced the Constitution, Delegate George Mason noted that members of Congress possessed “inquisitory powers” and “must meet frequently to inspect the Conduct of public officials.” Even though this idea was never written down, it was a habit of self-government that early Congresses put into practice.

Congressional oversight began almost as soon as the first Congress met. In 1790, Robert Morris, the superintendent of finances during the Continental Congress and a financier of the American Revolution, asked Congress to investigate his handling of the country’s finances and was exonerated of any wrongdoing.

During this period, congressional investigations were often referred to select committees – bodies created to perform special functions. These panels had the power to issue subpoenas and hold individuals in contempt. Since there was no official record of debates and proceedings, the public relied on newspaper accounts to learn about what had happened.

In March 1792, congressional oversight exposed businessman William Duer, who signed contracts with the War Department but failed to furnish the needed military supplies. This shortfall contributed to a stunning U.S. military defeat against a confederation of Native American tribes in the Northwest Territory.
Congress eventually removed the quartermaster general from his role for mismanaging the contracts.
Throughout the 19th century, Congress continued to quietly exercise this power.

Hearings from December 1861 to May 1865 on the conduct of the U.S. Civil War produced a detailed record of the war, exposed military wrongdoing and condemned slavery. In 1871, the Senate created a select committee to investigate Ku Klux Klan violence during Reconstruction.
Congress started to use its oversight power more aggressively in the 1920s with the Senate Committee on Public Land and Surveys’ high-profile investigations into the Teapot Dome scandal.

Hearings revealed that Interior Secretary Albert Bacon Fall had secretly leased federal oil reserves in Wyoming to two private corporations and had received personal loans and gifts from the companies in return.
The investigation found clear evidence of corruption. Fall was indicted and became the first U.S. Cabinet member to be convicted of a felony.

title: ‘Epic’ blue wave helps Democrats take Congress in overwhelming rebuke to President Trump
paragraphs: Voters turned out in massive numbers on Election Day to hand Democrats control of Congress, in a sweeping snub of President Donald Trump and Republicans. Democrats won several statewide races in places long considered GOP bastions, including races that were considered insurmountable even weeks ago.

Democrats took control of the House and Senate, flipping Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas and Ohio. The results reflected broad dissatisfaction across the country with Trump, his agenda and the candidates he had endorsed.
The Conversation’s senior politics editor, Alfonso Serrano, spoke on election night with Charlie Hunt, a scholar at Boise State University who studies Congress and elections.

It was obviously a strong showing for Democrats on Election Day, something that was even evident in the margin of some Democratic losses. What does it tell you, for example, that democratic socialist Angie Nixon fought a competitive race for the Senate in Florida?

There is this big uniform shift toward the Democrats that we’re seeing really across virtually all kinds of locations and geographies and counties. What I think is particularly notable here, and something we were on the lookout for in this election, and we’re seeing it, is the substantial shift in the Hispanic vote from 2024 in places like Texas and Florida, where you’re getting these 30-to-35 point shifts from how Donald Trump performed in 2024. That was a big part of what helped him win, and it seems like it has snapped right back and even farther in the other direction. This is what made Florida, I think, closer than a lot of folks thought.

It’s what put a number of really, really right-leaning districts in play, particularly in South Florida. And it looks like it is going to help Democrats keep the number of seats they had in Florida in the House that they had before the election, which is incredible when you consider that Florida did this mid-decade gerrymander to try to get them out of a bunch of those seats.

Some rural areas of the country were also more competitive than expected, like North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, where Democrat Jaime Ager flipped a conservative district. What does that tell you?

It’s definitely an indicator of at least one of these two things. One is just really massive Democratic turnout across the board. Regardless of where they live, Democrats were so enthusiastic and energized to turn out that they did so across all different types of districts and counties.

It could also be an indicator of some cross-party voting, where Republicans are crossing over in some cases and voting for the Democrat. I don’t imagine there’s a ton of that, but in a lot of these close districts, and if you’ve got enough of those folks in places like Texas, it really does make a big difference, those small shifts.

I think we’re probably also likely to see, and we saw some of this in the exit polling, a major shift in independent voters, unaffiliated voters, toward the Democrats, whereas in 2024 they had been closer to Trump.

I’d like to go back to turnout briefly. Turnout looks like it was strong across the country. In Georgia, for example, Election Day’s turnout was on pace to beat turnout in the 2024 presidential elections.

That’s unprecedented, at least in modern elections. In Texas, for example, in some counties we saw James Talarico getting as many raw votes as Kamala Harris did in a presidential election. This isn’t a very political science term, but that’s insane. In a midterm election you typically see 10% or 15% less turnout than you would in a presidential election. But Democrats voted in presidential-level numbers in a lot of these really key areas, and that’s explaining how they’re able to overperform at levels we haven’t seen in at least 20 years.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, including some US$200 million in Texas to elect Ken Paxton for the Senate, who lost. What does that tell you about the influence of political spending?

Republican PACs, super PACs and billionaire donors like Elon Musk may have raised more money compared to Democrats, but Democratic candidates themselves outraised Republican candidates through donors that gave directly to their campaigns.

This is important for a couple of reasons. Number one, because candidates get much better rates on TV ad buys than outside spenders. And so they get more bang for their buck when they’re spending on advertisements, which is the most expensive component of any campaign. And more to the point, that is an indicator of sort of dedicated grassroots donors who turn into voters, whereas Musk gets one vote at the end of the day.

And there is no amount of money that can make up for a really flawed candidate like Ken Paxton. And more to the point, a lot of this money, once you get into the tens, the hundreds of millions of dollars, a lot of the research talks about the diminishing returns that you get on that. Going from zero dollars spent to $10 million spent, that’s a very different kind of campaign. But once you go from $500 million to $510 million, that’s not going to get you a whole lot more votes.
Any final thoughts?

The territory that Democrats covered is unbelievable. The South Carolina Senate race went to Annie Andrews, the Democrat, which was unfathomable even a few months ago. Mississippi still appears to be somewhat in play. The blue wave turned into something approaching a tsunami. I think a lot of Democrats saw the polling and didn’t want to believe it or couldn’t bring themselves to believe it. But some of this late polling seems to have gotten things on the mark.

What we’ve seen in these midterm elections is a massive rebuke of the last two years of the Trump administration, and a sort of blue wave of epic proportions toward the Democrats, the likes of which we haven’t seen in 20 or more years. It’s a huge confirmation of the approach that Democrats took in this election.

Charlie Hunt does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Disaster aid has become a political lottery – libraries, schools and places of worship are stepping into the breach
paragraphs: Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again.

I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University, I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “Beyond Common Ground.”
The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet.
The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades.

Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states.
Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s.

Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the Panhandle, one of his “favorite places.” There, a January 2025 snowstorm was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages.

Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, compared with about 42% from states he lost.

While the White House has denied that politics plays a role in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025.

FEMA owes local governments almost $10 billion in reimbursements for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as 15% of their annual budget. Philanthropies and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps.
Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can build cooperation, trust and collective action, which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery.
In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the EF3 tornado that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors.
School administrators turned the local high school into a shelter the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund.
That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed.

Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them. A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents pay their insurance deductibles.
Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together.

After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, the figure hit only 45%. The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states.

My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll: bonding ties and linking ties.
Bonding ties connect neighbors and family.
Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans.
Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022.

Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan.

In my new book, I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery.

title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor
paragraphs: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated, and some are two decades old. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
The new research helps communities locate those homes.
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives, how well the building holds up, whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner. They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes, and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.
Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy, and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s, and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes, improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.
Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.
Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.

Yilei Yu receives support from Rice University’s Center for Coastal Futures and Adaptive Resilience and has received support from the School of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning at Arizona State University.

title: US wildfire damage is on pace to triple by mid-century, but there are affordable ways to lower the risk
paragraphs: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.S. is on pace to triple by mid-century, my colleagues and I found in a study just published.

The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive.

The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack, early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.

Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington, damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.

In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.

Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average. The U.S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually.

Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.

Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U.S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.

More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas, raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.
These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000.
They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires, which can overwhelm emergency response.

In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2.7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs.

A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.
The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U.S., raising the risk of damage.

Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold, increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.

My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060.

We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.

We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities. In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire.
These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.

For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris, mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.

Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0.6% and 4.2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.
Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it.

Beyond individual buildings, prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and reduce the probability of ignition while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can reward measurable risk reduction and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.

These measures work best when they reinforce one another. The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.
